claims.text: The material family of interest is multiphase refractory high-entropy alloys containing refractory elements such as W, Ta, Mo, Nb, and V, potentially alloyed with Al or Ti.
The primary mechanical property of interest is tensile ductility during and after aging.
These alloys will exhibit a ductile-brittle-ductile transition during aging at 400–700 °C.
The proposed non-monotonic transition results from ordered-phase formation followed by ordered-phase dissolution and recovery of matrix dislocation mobility.
Refractory high-entropy alloys generally have a BCC matrix and can contain dispersed secondary phases.
NbMoTaW- and NbMoTaWV-based refractory alloys are brittle at room temperature.
The initial limited ductility arises from coarse grain boundaries or inherent phase instability.
Intermediate-temperature aging for 10–1000 hours will induce chemical ordering and precipitation.
B2, Laves, and other intrinsically brittle secondary phases can limit ambient-temperature tensile ductility in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Coherent or semi-coherent B2- or L12-type nanoprecipitates initially pin dislocations and cause embrittlement.
Coarsening or dissolution of ordered precipitates restores dislocation glide and ductility.
Ordered precipitates increase yield strength while reducing ductility by promoting brittle fracture.
Thermally activated dislocation cross-slip at longer aging times or higher temperatures restores plasticity.
Coherent nanoprecipitation can overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys.
Ductility will first decrease to a distinct minimum and then recover as aging proceeds.
Yield strength will peak at an intermediate aging time.
Unaged multiphase refractory high-entropy alloys and conventional refractory alloys typically show monotonic ductility degradation with aging or remain brittle without recovery.
The transition requires compositions capable of forming metastable ordered phases, such as refractory matrices containing Al, Ti, or Ni.
The transition is bounded to temperatures below approximately 700 °C where the ordered phase remains thermodynamically stable.
Initial grain size and defect density produced by additive manufacturing or casting can alter the onset of ordering.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as already brittle or only weakly ductile, whereas a ductile-brittle-ductile sequence and an initial sharp ductility drop require a meaningfully ductile starting state.

The aging treatment is specified to remain below the solvus and avoid complete dissolution, but precipitate dissolution is also presented as a principal cause of late-stage ductility recovery without clarifying whether only partial dissolution is intended.

The ordered phase is described as thermodynamically stable below about 700 °C, while the proposed transition within 400–700 °C relies in part on that phase dissolving. No thermodynamic or kinetic condition reconciling stability with dissolution is given.
